verdict.rationale: The canon lexically does not name Halloween or any similar late-autumn observance, so the verdict is reached by composition (by combining several lines of evidence rather than one direct verse). The first clause of the proposition, rejecting occult and death-glorifying practice, sits on a dense, spread-across-the-whole-Bible (pan-canonical) occult wordstock: 'abomination' (toebah), 'divination' (nachash), 'sorcery' (kashaph), 'medium' (ob), 'familiar spirit' (yiddeoni), 'one who inquires of the dead' (darash el hammethim) in Deuteronomy 18:9-12, and 'have joint fellowship' (synkoinoneo) with the 'unfruitful works of darkness' (akarpa erga tou skotous) in Ephesians 5:11, reinforced by 1 Corinthians 10:20-21 where pagan ritual is offered to 'demons' (daimonia) and incompatible with the cup and table of the Lord. The second clause, that otherwise harmless cultural participation is a matter of conscience, has no single Bible word that names a calendar custom; it rests on the general criterion 'to the glory of God' (eis doxan theou) in 1 Corinthians 10:31, the conscience vocabulary of 1 Corinthians 8 ('conscience' syneidesis, 'food sacrificed to idols' eidolothuton, 'liberty' exousia, 'stumbling block' proskomma), and the day-judging clause of Romans 14:5-6 ('day' hemera, 'judge' krino, 'each' ekastos, 'be fully convinced' plerophoreo) plus Colossians 2:16 ('festival' heorte, 'new moon' noumenia, 'sabbath' sabbaton). Because the wordstock decides the occult side cleanly but lets the application-level conscience side stand on a general standard rather than a named permission or prohibition, the composite proposition is lexically contested at exactly the seam where readers diverge.

scripture.force: The verse opens the unit by forbidding Israel to learn to do according to the 'abominations' (toebah) of the 'nations' (goyim), framing the whole following catalog as gentile occult practice that is categorically off limits, not as morally indifferent custom.

A chain of negated participial agents (verb forms acting as nouns, like 'one who does X'), 'one who practices divination' (qosem qesamim), 'a diviner' working through omen-reading (menahesh, from nachash), 'a sorcerer' working through magic (mekhasheph, from kashaph), and 'the one who makes his son or daughter pass through the fire' (esh), enumerates concrete occult and death-dealing acts. The passing-through-fire clause ties the prohibition to ritual that takes life and yokes the prohibition explicitly to death-glorifying practice.

The clause 'one who inquires of the dead' (doresh el hammethim, from darash 'to inquire' and muth 'to die'), together with 'medium' (ob), 'familiar spirit' (yiddeoni), and 'a binder of spells' (chober chaber), targets necromancy (consulting the dead) and contact with the dead. This is the closest single-word match inside the canon to the death-glorifying aspect of the proposition, and it is condemned outright. The same cluster recurs in Leviticus 19:31, Leviticus 20:6, Leviticus 20:27, 1 Samuel 28:3-9, 2 Kings 21:6, 2 Kings 23:24, Isaiah 8:19, and Isaiah 19:3, giving the prohibition a spread-across-the-whole-Old-Testament (pan-canonical OT) footprint.

Summary verdict: 'everyone (kol) doing these things is an abomination (toebah) to the LORD' (kol oseh elleh toabath YHWH), and on account of these abominations the nations are being dispossessed. The universal scope of 'every' (kol) and the covenant judgment seal the prohibition as absolute for every occult act named in verses 10-11.

'Do not have joint fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness' (me synkoinoneite tois ergois tois akarpois tou skotous): do not 'have joint fellowship' (synkoinoneo, a rare verb of shared participation occurring only here, Philippians 4:14, and Revelation 18:4) with the 'unfruitful' (akarpos) 'works' (erga) of 'darkness' (skotos), but rather 'expose' (elegcho) them. The command bars shared participation in any pattern characterized by darkness and barrenness, supporting rejection of the occult dimension, but it defines darkness morally (as 'fruitless', akarpos) rather than by any calendar marker, so its application to a named holiday is mediated (one step removed), not direct.

'What they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God' (ha thuousin, daimoniois thuousin kai ou theo), that is, to 'demons' (daimonia). Paul reframes pagan religious acts as actually directed to demonic powers, not merely to nothing, which sharpens the occult-rejection side of the proposition by giving the spiritual rationale for the Deuteronomy 18 ban.

'You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons' (ou dynasthe poterion kyriou pinein kai poterion daimonion), nor 'partake of' (metechein) the table of the Lord and the table of 'demons' (daimonia). The 'you cannot' (dynasthe) construction states a categorical impossibility for cultic participation in both spheres, locking the occult-rejection clause as absolute when the act is actually religious sharing with 'demons' (daimonia).

'Whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God' (eite oun esthiete eite pinete eite ti poieite, panta eis doxan theou poieite), that is, all to the 'glory' (doxa) of God. The 'whether-whether-all' (eite-eite-panta) construction supplies a comprehensive God-honoring (doxological) test governing all conduct, but names no holiday and at the word level neither affirms nor forbids a specific cultural custom. It can ground a conscience reading only by application, not by direct single-word match, which is the seam where readers diverge.

'One judges one day above another, another judges every day alike, let each be fully convinced in his own mind' (hos men gar krinei hemeran par hemeran, hos de krinei pasan hemeran, hekastos en to idio noi plerophoreistho): one 'judges' (krino) one 'day' (hemera) above another, another 'judges' (krino) every 'day' (hemera) alike, let 'each' (hekastos) be 'fully convinced' (plerophoreo) in his own 'mind' (nous). The grammar privatizes (makes a private matter of) the day-judgment to the individual conscience formed before God. The word 'be fully convinced' (plerophoreo), attested only 6 times in the canon, is the key verb for the conscience-formation step and is the direct word-level hook for the proposition's matter-of-conscience clause, though it does not name any specific holiday.

'Let no one judge you about food or drink or in respect of a festival or new moon or sabbath' (me oun tis hymas krineto en brosei kai en posei e en merei heortes e noumenias e sabbaton): that is, no one is to 'judge' (krino) you regarding a 'festival' (heorte), a 'new moon' (noumenia, a New Testament hapax, meaning a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, found only here), or 'sabbath' (sabbaton). The prohibition on inter-personal day-judgment is explicit, and 'festival' (heorte) is a word-level named festival category, so this passage provides the closest available New Testament word for general festival liberty. But the named festivals are Jewish calendar items, not pagan-origin observances, so the analogy to a contested cultural-origin holiday is by extension, not by direct denotation (direct word-for-thing match).

'But not everyone has this knowledge; some, accustomed until now to the idol, eat the food as if it were truly offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled' (all ouk en pasin he gnosis, tines de te synetheia heos arti tou eidolou hos eidolothuton esthiousin, kai he syneidesis auton asthenes ousa molynetai): their 'conscience' (syneidesis) is defiled. The word 'conscience' (syneidesis), together with 'food sacrificed to idols' (eidolothuton), supplies the New Testament vocabulary for a cultural-religious participation question that depends on conscience and knowledge rather than on a bright-line ban. This is the closest New Testament analogue to a participation-with-discernment reading.

'See that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak' (blepete de mepos he exousia hymon haute proskomma genetai tois asthenesin): see that this 'liberty' (exousia) of yours does not become a 'stumbling block' (proskomma) to the weak. The text affirms a real Christian 'liberty' (exousia) in such matters yet binds it by neighbor-love, which is the lexical (word-level) shape of the conscience-with-discernment reading.

complicating_texts.resolution: The 'to the glory of God' (eis doxan theou) rule is comprehensive but criterial (it sets a test, not a list of permitted acts), not casuistic (case-by-case). It supplies a test for any act yet names no calendar custom, so it can support a conscience carve-out only by application. The word itself leaves the harmless-participation clause undetermined, which is why the composite proposition is rated disputed rather than affirmed.

Direct query of the word-level data confirms Romans 14:5 contains G2250 'day' (hemera), G2919 'judge' (krino), G1538 'each' (hekastos), G3563 'mind' (nous), and the rare G4135 'be fully convinced' (plerophoreo). The grammar privatizes (makes a private matter of) day-judgment to the individual conscience, supporting a matter-of-conscience reading on day observances. But Paul addresses Jewish vs gentile calendar disputes in a Roman house-church, and no Bible word names a pagan-origin holiday, so the application to a culturally contested observance is by extension, not by direct denotation. This is why the second clause of the proposition is lexically (word-level) supported but not lexically determined.

Colossians 2:16 forbids inter-personal judging on 'festival' (heorte), 'new moon' (noumenia, a New Testament hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), and 'sabbath' (sabbaton), and so generalizes the day-liberty principle beyond Romans 14. But the festival category in view is Mosaic-cycle observance, not pagan-origin observance, and 'new moon' (noumenia) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) with no other canon disambiguation, so a clean application to Halloween requires an inference the wordstock does not itself perform.

Paul says pagan sacrifice is offered to 'demons' (daimonia, Strong's G1140, with 63 New Testament occurrences, semantically stable as malevolent spiritual beings) and not to God, and one cannot share the cup and the table of demons. This sharpens the rejection clause as a categorical impossibility for actually-religious participation in occult or demonic ritual. It does not weaken the rejection half of the verdict; it strengthens it.

1 Corinthians 8 introduces 'conscience' (syneidesis, with 30 New Testament occurrences) and 'food offered to idols' (eidolothuton, with 9 occurrences, confined to 1 Corinthians 8, 1 Corinthians 10, Acts 15, Revelation 2). Paul rules that the idol is nothing yet binds the strong person's 'liberty' (exousia) by the weak brother's 'stumbling block' (proskomma). At the word level this is the closest New Testament analogue to a culturally-tinged participation question, but the named referent is meat from pagan sacrifice, not a calendar custom, so it grounds the principle without naming Halloween.

variants.note: No variant units (places where ancient manuscripts disagree) were supplied for the cited verses. Ephesians 5:11, Romans 14:5, Colossians 2:16, 1 Corinthians 8, and 1 Corinthians 10 are New Testament passages outside 3 John, so CBGM (the coherence-based genealogical method, a manuscript-relationship tool) is treated as shadow only (background reference, not decisive) and the verdict does not turn on any contested reading.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: affirms the rejection clause, leaves the conscience clause open
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading Deuteronomy 18:9-12 as an enduring moral prohibition on occult practice and consultation of the dead, carried forward by Ephesians 5:11 and 1 Corinthians 10:20-21, yields a firm no on the occult and death-glorifying half. The same lens says nothing decisive about indifferent custom, so it leaves the second clause genuinely open rather than answered.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: affirms the conscience clause as a legitimate application
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading 1 Corinthians 8 through 10 plus Romans 14:5-6 and Colossians 2:16 as establishing real 'liberty' (exousia) in things 'indifferent' (adiaphora, matters neither commanded nor forbidden) supports treating non-occult cultural participation as a matter of individual conscience under the God-honoring (doxological) rule of 1 Corinthians 10:31. This lens depends on an application step the wordstock supplies in principle but not by direct denotation (direct word-for-thing match), which is the contested join.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: treats the conscience clause as a category error
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading Ephesians 5:11 strictly (do not even share fellowship with the works of darkness, but expose them) together with the pagan-origin character of Samhain-derived practice (Samhain being the ancient Celtic festival from which Halloween descends) argues that nothing once shaped by death-ritual is recoverable as indifferent custom. On this lens the proposition's second clause concedes too much to cultural participation. The word 'have joint fellowship' (synkoinoneo) is rare (3 New Testament occurrences) and morally absolute in tone, which fairly supports this reading even if it does not force it.

hermeneutics.notes: The two clauses of the proposition are governed by different word-level centers. The prohibition rests on a dense, spread-across-the-whole-Bible (pan-canonical) occult vocabulary: 'abomination' (toebah), 'medium' (ob), 'familiar spirit' (yiddeoni), 'divination' (nachash), 'sorcery' (kashaph), 'demon' (daimonion). The conscience carve-out rests on general criteria and word-level analogues: 'to the glory of God' (eis doxan theou), 'conscience' (syneidesis), 'liberty' (exousia), 'be fully convinced' (plerophoreo), 'festival' (heorte) that, while real, do not name pagan-origin calendar customs. The verdict turns on whether the second clause counts as a legitimate application of named principles or as an unwarranted extension into a category the canon never names directly.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: How does the canonical wordstock treat participation in occult or death-related ritual, and does it license, forbid, or leave open participation in cultural customs of pagan-religious origin that the participant judges otherwise harmless.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem preloads a verdict by partitioning Halloween into rejected occult and death-glorifying aspects versus a permitted harmless category that is declared a matter of conscience. The terms 'harmless' and 'matter of conscience' encode the conclusion of the second clause before the lexeme (the specific Bible word) is consulted. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form separates the empirical word-level question from the embedded conclusion. VERDICT-CHANGED: No verdict change from the prior file; the prior disputed verdict is confirmed by the deeper query, which adds Romans 14:5, Colossians 2:16, 1 Corinthians 8:7, 1 Corinthians 8:9, and 1 Corinthians 10:20-21 as resolving word-level anchors for both lenses.

lay_summary: The canon does not name Halloween, so the verdict is reached by composition (by combining several lines of evidence). On the rejection side the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 18:9-12 stacks a precise occult vocabulary: 'divination' (nachash), 'sorcery' (kashaph), a 'medium' (ob), a 'familiar spirit' (yiddeoni), 'inquiring' (darash) of 'the dead' (muth), and one who passes a child through the fire. The whole list is sealed by 'abomination' (toebah) and by the statement that 'everyone' (kol) doing these things is detestable to the LORD. The same word cluster recurs in Leviticus, 1 Samuel 28, 2 Kings, and Isaiah, giving the prohibition reach across the whole Bible. In the New Testament Ephesians 5:11 uses the rare verb 'have joint fellowship' (synkoinoneo), attested only three times, and tells readers not to share in the 'unfruitful' (akarpos) 'works of darkness' (skotos) but instead to 'expose' (elegcho) them. 1 Corinthians 10:20-21 sharpens this: pagan ritual is offered to 'demons' (daimonia), and you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. The first clause of the proposition, that occult and death-glorifying activity is rejected, sits on firm word-level ground across both Testaments. The second clause, that harmless cultural participation is a matter of conscience, has no Bible word that names a calendar custom. It rests on the comprehensive 'to the glory of God' (eis doxan theou) rule of 1 Corinthians 10:31, on the conscience vocabulary of 1 Corinthians 8 ('conscience' syneidesis, 'food sacrificed to idols' eidolothuton, 'liberty' exousia, 'stumbling block' proskomma), on the day-judgment grammar of Romans 14:5-6 where 'each' (hekastos) is to be 'fully convinced' (plerophoreo, only 6 canon uses) in his own mind, and on Colossians 2:16 which forbids inter-personal judging about 'festival' (heorte) and 'new moon' (noumenia, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, attested only here). Each of these is genuine word-level material, but none denote a pagan-origin observance. The wordstock decides the occult side clearly. It supplies principles, not direct word-for-thing matches, for the cultural side. That is the word-level root of the disagreement: the same canon yields a categorical no to actual occult and demonic communion and a principled but unnamed yes to liberty under conscience, and the proposition welds them at exactly the seam the words leave open.
